name: Fundamentals of Computing
description: This is an introductory C course that covered the fundamentals up to and including pointers. Example projects are a Conway's Game of Life simulator, a crossword puzzle generator, fractal designs, and a final project, for which I remade Tetris using X11 graphics. Click on the gif to download it yourself (I still play it from time to time)!

name: Abstract Algebra
description: This is a traditional abstract algebra course that studies groups, rings and fields. The class covered permutations, modular arithmetic, cryptography, cyclic and dihedral groups, Lagrange's theorem, homomorphisms, ideals, and integral domains. My final paper for the class researched Boolean algebras and culminated in a proof of isomorphism between Boolean algebras, Boolean rings, and the power set.

name: Theory of Computing
description:
This course introduced computability theory, formal languages and automata, and complexity theory with the goal of understanding the limits of various computational models such as finite automata, pushdown automata, context-free grammars, and Turing machines. Some topics we covered were undecidability, the classes P and NP, reduction, and NP completeness.

For the class, I designed in a group a nondeterministic finite automata simulator, a regular expression parser and matcher similar to grep which uses that NFA simulator, a sed-like editor with a complimentary Turing machine simulator, and a regex matcher with backreferences. We also proved the regex matcher with backreferences was NP-complete by building a SAT solver through regular expression matching with backreferences.

name: Operating Systems Principles
description: Covered three important themes of operating systems—virtualization, concurrency, and persistence—via system calls, OS scheduling and different scheduling algorithms, concurrency via events, threads, locks, and sempahores, paging, segmentation, file systems, disks, flash, RAID, and more. Projects include a process queue shell in C simulates FIFO, Round Robin, and MLFQ scheduling on multiple cores; a chat client that threads sending and receiving messages; an implementation of malloc; and a miniature user-space file system.

name: Passage to Italy
description: This is a fifth-semester Italian class to refine grammar and understand Italian culture from the 11th century onward. I read literature from ancient authors (e.g. Dante, Cavalcanti, San Francesco d'Assisi), analyzed art of the Renaissance and Baroque periods (e.g. Michelangelo, Raffaelo, Caravaggio), compared those eras to recent authors and art movements (Leopardi, Primo Levi, futurismo) and studied Italian history to boot (reunification, Risorgimento). Check out my final paper, a comparison of Michelangelo's Pietà, here.

name: Compilers and Language Design
description: Built a compiler for a safe, compiled, statically-typed C-like language called B-minor. We covered parsing theory, various complexities of grammars, and development tools like Flex and Bison/Yacc. Through Bison's parsing, hand-crafted type checking (much harder than expected) and x86 code generation, the compiler produced assembly interoperable with C. While it took a long time, generating code for just iterating over a loop was very satisfying. See the project here.

name: Undergraduate Research in Computer Graphics
description: Under Professor Daniel Rehberg, worked on a project simulating Aeolian sand simulations through OpenGL with 3 other undergraduates. Through this project, I was first exposed to creating pull requests and studying the graphics pipeline in full. Beyond study, I wrote many vertex, fragment, geometry, and tessellation shaders, experimented with SDL3, implemented lighting and dynamic tessellation, and generating some sand graphics that took advantage of the dynamic simulation of the project.
